title: The p-value
objectives: Compute a p-value and say exactly what it is a probability of.

screens.title: How much of the curve?
screens.prose: Last lesson’s strategy had $z = 1.054$. If it has no skill, $z$ comes from this $N(0, 1)$ curve. The shaded tail holds every $z$ at least as large as 1.054.
screens.question: Roughly what share of the area under the curve is shaded?

options.why: You judged by the thin far end of the tail. Near $z = 1$ the curve is still tall.
Half the area lies above 0, not above 1.054.
That is the unshaded part, below 1.054.

hints.text: The whole area under the curve is 1. Is the shaded part closer to a tenth or to a half?
Compare the tail with the half of the curve above 0.
About one sd above the mean, a normal curve leaves roughly 16% in the upper tail.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The whole area is 1; judge how much of it lies beyond 1.054.

explain.text: The shaded area is 0.146, about 15%. Luck alone gives a $z$ this large about one time in seven. That area is the number this lesson is about.

screens.title: A tail of 5%
screens.prose: Slide the cut-off $z$. The label is the area of the tail beyond it: the chance, under $H_0$, of a $z$ at least that large.
screens.question: Find the cut-off whose upper tail is as close to 0.05 as you can get. What is it?

widget.label: Cut-off z
widget.accept: 1.64 or 1.65: the exact value is 1.645, where the upper tail is 0.0500.

hints.text: Slide right until the label reads close to 0.0500.
Watch the tail label shrink as the cut-off moves right.
At 1.64 the tail is 0.0505; at 1.65 it is 0.0495.

feedback.correct: At about 1.645 the upper tail is 0.05.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Stop where the tail label is closest to 0.0500, and give the cut-off.

byKey.two-sided: At 1.96 the upper tail is 0.025, not 0.05. That cut-off splits 5% between two tails.
byKey.tail: That is the tail area. The question asks for the cut-off $z$ itself.

explain.text: The upper tail is 0.05 at $z = 1.645$: the one-sided cut-off at 5%. The familiar 1.96 puts 0.025 in each of two tails. Which one applies depends on $H_1$.

screens.title: The p-value
screens.prose: The tail area is the **p-value**: the chance, if $H_0$ is true, of a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. With $H_1: \mu > \mu_0$, “extreme” means large: $$p = P(Z \ge z \mid H_0) = 1 - \Phi(z).$$
screens.question: What is the one-sided p-value for the strategy, with $z = 1.054$?

hints.text: $\Phi(z)$ is the area below $z$. Which part do you want?
The p-value is the shaded tail.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the area above $z$: $1 - \Phi(z)$.

byKey.phi: That is $\Phi(1.054)$, the area below $z$. The p-value is the tail above it.
byKey.doubled: You doubled the tail, which is the two-sided p-value. This $H_1$ is one-sided.

explain.text: The tail above 1.054 has area $1 - 0.854 = 0.146$. So if the strategy had no skill, luck would give a $z$ this large 14.6% of the time. That is the one-sided p-value.

screens.title: Both tails
screens.prose: Suppose the test had been two-sided, $H_1: \mu \ne 0$. Then $z = -1.054$ would be just as extreme as $1.054$, so both tails count: $$p = P(|Z| \ge |z|) = 2\left(1 - \Phi(|z|)\right).$$
screens.question: What is the two-sided p-value for the strategy?

hints.text: Each tail has the same area. You found one of them on the last screen.
Both shaded tails count now.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the areas of both tails.

byKey.one-tail: That is one tail. A two-sided test counts $z \le -1.054$ as well.
byKey.halved: You halved the tail. Two-sided adds the other tail, so $p$ grows.
byKey.middle: That is the unshaded middle. The p-value is the two tails.

explain.text: Both tails have area 0.146, so the two-sided p-value is 0.292. The same data give twice the p-value under the two-sided question. The strategy’s $z$ is unremarkable either way.

screens.title: Reject or not
screens.prose: The fill-rate change gave $z = 1.936$. Before looking, the desk fixed a two-sided test at **level** $\alpha = 0.05$. The rule: **reject $H_0$** if $p \le \alpha$, otherwise **fail to reject**. Here $p = 2(1 - \Phi(1.936)) = 0.0529$.
screens.question: What is the decision?

options.why: Almost is not past. The rule was fixed before the data: reject only if $p \le 0.05$.
Failing to reject is not accepting. The data are close to surprising; they just fall short.

options.text: Reject $H_0$, since the one-sided p-value is 0.026
options.why: You switched to one-sided after seeing the data. That halves $p$ unfairly; the test was declared two-sided.

hints.text: Compare $p$ with $\alpha$.
Each tail holds 0.0264; together they hold 0.0529.
$0.0529$ is just above $0.05$, so the rule says do not reject.

feedback.correct: $p = 0.0529$ is just above 0.05: fail to reject.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the rule fixed in advance: reject only if $p \le 0.05$.

explain.text: The two tails hold $0.0264 + 0.0264 = 0.0529$, just above 0.05, so we fail to reject. That does not show the change did nothing. More orders would settle it.

screens.title: The largest p-value
screens.prose: Slide the observed $z$ and watch the two-sided p-value in the caption.
screens.question: Slide $z$ to make the two-sided p-value as large as it can be.

hints.text: The p-value grows as the tails grow. Where are they largest?
The tails start at $-|z|$ and $|z|$.
Put $z$ at the centre, 0.

feedback.correct: At $z = 0$ the two tails cover the whole curve: $p = 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move $z$ until the two tails meet.

byKey.far: You moved away from the centre, so the tails, and $p$, shrank.
byKey.far-low: You moved away from the centre, so the tails, and $p$, shrank.

explain.text: At $z = 0$ each tail is half the curve, so $p = 2(1 - \Phi(0)) = 1$. Data exactly at the null mean are as unsurprising as data can be. Even $p = 1$ does not prove $H_0$.

screens.title: A probability of what?
screens.prose: For the fill-rate change, $p = 0.0529$. A colleague writes: “So there is a 5.3% chance the change did nothing.”

state.caption: This curve is drawn assuming $H_0$ is true

screens.question: Is that what $p = 0.0529$ means?

options.text: No: it is the chance of data at least this extreme if the change did nothing
Yes: a p-value is the chance that $H_0$ is true
options.why: You swapped the condition. $p$ is $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$, not $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$: the prosecutor’s fallacy again.

options.text: No: it means a 94.7% chance the change worked
options.why: You read $1 - p$ as the chance of $H_1$. The curve assumes $H_0$, so it gives no chance for $H_1$ at all.

options.text: No: it is the chance the next 1,000 orders show the same rise
options.why: A p-value describes data under $H_0$. It says nothing about what a repeat would show.

hints.text: Which hypothesis was assumed to draw the curve?
The shaded tails are areas under the null curve.
The p-value is $P(|Z| \ge 1.936 \mid H_0)$. Read the condition after the bar.

feedback.correct: It is a chance about the data, computed as if $H_0$ were true.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what was assumed in order to compute 0.0529.

byKey.swap: You swapped the condition. $p$ is $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$, not $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$: the prosecutor’s fallacy again.
byKey.one-minus: You read $1 - p$ as the chance of $H_1$. The curve assumes $H_0$, so it gives no chance for $H_1$ at all.

explain.text: The p-value assumes $H_0$ and asks how often data this extreme would appear: $P(|Z| \ge 1.936 \mid H_0) = 0.0529$. The chance that $H_0$ is true would need a prior, as Bayes’ rule showed. The next level returns to these misreadings.

screens.title: p-values for any z test
screens.prose: You computed tails under the null curve. For an observed $z$: $$p = \begin{cases} 1 - \Phi(z) & H_1: \mu > \mu_0 \\ \Phi(z) & H_1: \mu < \mu_0 \\ 2\left(1 - \Phi(|z|)\right) & H_1: \mu \ne \mu_0 \end{cases}$$ Fix $\alpha$ first, then reject $H_0$ if $p \le \alpha$.
screens.question: A two-sided test gives $z = -2.2$. Which expression is its p-value?

options.why: You took the area above −2.2, about 0.986. A two-sided test uses the size $|z| = 2.2$.
You took one tail, 0.0139. A two-sided test counts both.
You doubled the area below 2.2, which is more than 1. No chance can be.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two-sided: double the tail beyond $|z|$.

screens.title: A p-value function
screens.prose: A research notebook needs a p-value for every $z$ it prints. Complete `p_value`. The helper `phi` is $\Phi(z) = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(1 + \text{erf}(z/\sqrt 2)\right)$, built from `math.erf`. One-sided means $H_1: \mu > \mu_0$.
screens.question: Complete `p_value(z, two_sided=True)`.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. Each answer is accepted when math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9). This is pure Python, so no package loads; the first run still starts Python, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: One-sided: the area above $z$. Two-sided: double the area beyond $|z|$.
The upper tail is `1 - phi(z)`. For two-sided, use `abs(z)`.
Return `2 * (1 - phi(abs(z)))` when two-sided, else `1 - phi(z)`.

feedback.correct: Both tails beyond $|z|$, or the one tail above $z$.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check a negative $z$: a two-sided p-value must not change sign.

byKey.test-1: For $z = 1.054$, two-sided, the answer is 0.2919. Double the upper tail beyond $|z|$.
byKey.test-4: For $z = -1.936$ the two-sided answer equals that for 1.936. Use `abs(z)`.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace each `...` with an expression.

explain.text: `1 - phi(z)` is the upper tail, and doubling the tail beyond `abs(z)` gives the two-sided value. So $p(1.054) = 0.2919$ and $p(0) = 1$. One-sided at $z = -1.054$ gives 0.854: data on the wrong side are no evidence for $H_1$.

screens.title: Exact or approximate?
screens.prose: Back to 14 wins in 20 trades. The exact one-sided p-value is $P(W \ge 14) = 0.0577$. The normal curve with mean 10 and sd $\sqrt 5$ approximates the bars. Each bar spans half a win either side, so the tail starts at 13.5.
screens.question: Use the normal curve from 13.5 upward, with $\Phi(1.565) = 0.9412$. What p-value does it give?

hints.text: Standardise 13.5: subtract the mean 10, then divide by $\sqrt 5 \approx 2.236$.
The coloured bars start at 14, so the curve’s tail starts half a win earlier.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start the tail at 13.5, standardise, then take $1 - \Phi$.

byKey.no-correction: You started the tail at 14. That skips the left half of the 14 bar, so $p$ comes out too small.
byKey.exact: That is the exact binomial value. The question asks what the normal curve gives.
byKey.phi: That is $\Phi(1.565)$, the area below. Take the tail above.

explain.text: With the half-win correction, $z = (13.5 - 10)/\sqrt 5 = 1.565$ and $p = 1 - 0.9412 = 0.0588$. The exact value is 0.0577, so the approximation is close. Starting at 14 instead gives $p = 0.0368$, far too small.

ideas: The p-value is the chance, assuming $H_0$, of a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.
One-sided: $p = 1 - \Phi(z)$. Two-sided: $p = 2(1 - \Phi(|z|))$. At $z = 0$ the two-sided $p$ is 1.
Fix the level $\alpha$ in advance. Reject $H_0$ if $p \le \alpha$; otherwise fail to reject, which is not accepting $H_0$.

formula.name: Two-sided p-value
formula.note: A chance about the data, computed as if $H_0$ were true.

summary.trap: A p-value is not the chance that $H_0$ is true, and $1 - p$ is not the chance that $H_1$ is true.

quiz.prose: A one-sided test with $H_1: \mu > \mu_0$ gives $z = 2.33$. You are told $\Phi(2.33) = 0.9901$.
quiz.question: What is the p-value?

byKey.phi: That is the area below $z$. The p-value is the tail above it.
byKey.doubled: You doubled the tail. This test is one-sided.

explain.text: The upper tail beyond 2.33 is $1 - 0.9901 = 0.0099$. Luck alone gives a $z$ this large about one time in 100.

quiz.prose: A two-sided test gives $z = -1.5$. You are told $\Phi(1.5) = 0.9332$.
quiz.question: What is the p-value?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Double the tail beyond $|z| = 1.5$.

byKey.one-tail: That is one tail. A two-sided test counts both.
byKey.middle: That is the area between −1.5 and 1.5. The p-value is outside it.

explain.text: The tail beyond 1.5 is $1 - 0.9332 = 0.0668$, and the sign of $z$ does not matter. Both tails give $p = 0.1336$.

quiz.prose: A backtest of a signal gives $p = 0.03$ for $H_0$: the signal has no edge.
quiz.question: Which statement is exactly right?

options.text: If the signal had no edge, results at least this extreme would occur 3% of the time
There is a 3% chance the signal has no edge
options.why: You read $p$ as $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$. It is computed assuming $H_0$, so it cannot be the chance of $H_0$.

options.text: There is a 97% chance the signal has an edge
options.why: You took $1 - p$ as the chance of $H_1$. No such chance comes out of a test.

options.text: The signal will lose money 3% of the time
options.why: A p-value is not a forecast of losses. It describes data under $H_0$.

feedback.correct: A chance about data, assuming no edge.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the p-value as $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$.

explain.text: The p-value is $P(\text{a result this extreme} \mid H_0)$. Under no edge, such a result turns up 3% of the time. The chance there is no edge would need Bayes’ rule and a prior.

quiz.prose: A risk committee fixed $\alpha = 0.01$ before a test. The test gives $p = 0.03$.
quiz.question: What is the decision?

options.why: You used 0.05. The committee fixed $\alpha = 0.01$ in advance.
Failing to reject is not accepting. The data are simply not extreme enough for this level.
You moved the level after seeing $p$. A level chosen after the data means nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $p$ with the level fixed in advance.

explain.text: The rule is reject when $p \le \alpha$. Here $0.03 > 0.01$, so we fail to reject. At the stricter level, this evidence is not enough.
